content: NOAA needs the NPOESS Data Exploitation system to turn polar-orbiting satellite observations into products for operational, climate, and other civilian users. The system should receive source data, generate standard and NOAA-specific products, package and distribute them to authorized customers, and deliver selected products to the long-term archive. It should also support registration, order status, product assistance, integrity monitoring, and continuity during failures.

The main business outcome is to turn raw polar satellite observations into trusted data products that NOAA and other authorized users can actually use for operations, climate monitoring, and public service missions. In practice, that means getting the right products out quickly, accurately, and reliably, so forecasters, analysts, and downstream systems can depend on them.
The user value is in timely access, consistency, and traceability. People need products they can order or receive with confidence, know whether their request is being processed, and have support if something looks wrong, while NOAA also needs selected data preserved in the long-term archive for future use.

Operationally, it needs to support products that can be used quickly for weather and environmental decision-making, so timeliness and reliability matter a lot. For climate, the system should preserve consistency and traceability so products can be used for long-term trend analysis and reprocessing if needed. For civilian users, it should provide the NOAA-specific and standard products they need in a usable form, with clear ordering, distribution, and support around access and status.

Yes, we have to assume the source data won’t always be perfectly continuous, so the system needs to handle gaps, delayed arrivals, and occasional degraded input without losing control of the product flow. Coverage will depend on the satellite pass and what the sensor actually captured, so products may be incomplete in some cases and still need to be distributed with that status clearly known. Latency is also a real constraint for the operational side, so the system has to produce and deliver time-sensitive products as soon as practical rather than waiting for ideal conditions.

At the top of the list, I’d put receiving the source data and generating the standard and NOAA-specific products correctly. Right after that, the system has to package and distribute those products to authorized users and send selected products to the long-term archive. We also need the basic support functions in place, especially registration, order status, product assistance, integrity monitoring, and continuity during failures.

The main external exchange is with NOAA and other authorized civilian users who receive the products, either through direct distribution or ordering. We also need to send selected products to the long-term archive, so that archive system is a key partner even if it’s more of a downstream repository than an active user. Beyond that, there may be upstream satellite or mission data providers involved in getting the source observations in, but I’d need to verify the exact interfaces and partner names with the program team.

We definitely need secure, controlled exchange because some products are only for authorized customers, but I don’t have the exact protocols pinned down yet. My expectation is that we’ll need standard, well-supported interfaces for product delivery and ordering, with authentication and access control, and probably integrity checks so users can verify what they received. If there are specific NOAA or archive transport standards we have to follow, I’d want to confirm those with the technical and security leads.

The main customer groups are NOAA operational users, climate and research users, and other civilian users who are authorized to receive specific products. Operational users usually need the fastest access and the most reliable delivery, while climate users care more about completeness, consistency, and long-term availability. Some products may be broadly available, but others will need tighter access controls depending on policy, licensing, or sensitivity.

Registration should not be completely open; eligibility depends on whether the requester is an authorized customer for the products they want. In practice, some users may be able to self-register for basic access, but higher-sensitivity or restricted products would need approval and role-based authorization before access is granted. I don’t have the exact approval matrix yet, so that would need to be confirmed with policy and security owners.

For restricted products, I’d expect approval to go through a designated NOAA program or product owner, with security or data stewardship reviewing the request when needed. They would check whether the requester is in the right organization, has the right role, and has a legitimate operational or research need for that product. Emergency or mission-critical access might be expedited, but I’d want those exceptions defined carefully so they’re controlled and auditable.

We’d want the system to generate products normally when the incoming source data meets the expected quality and completeness thresholds for that product. If the data is incomplete, corrupted, late, or fails validation, the product should either be held for reprocessing, corrected if the issue can be fixed automatically, or flagged as unusable if it can’t be trusted. The exact thresholds and correction rules are going to be product-specific, so those would need to come from the science and operations teams.

Support should cover help finding products, understanding product content and format, tracking order status, and basic troubleshooting when a delivery fails or a file looks wrong. Users should be able to request help through whatever customer service channel we set up, and the system should tie that request to the product and order so support can respond efficiently. Anything involving policy decisions, restricted access, or technical integrity failures that could affect multiple users should probably be routed to a separate operations or security path rather than handled as routine user support.

The ingest process should accept the source data formats that come from the satellite mission feed and whatever standard metadata is required to identify the observation, time, instrument, and processing lineage. I don’t know the exact file or message formats yet, but we would expect the system to validate that the metadata is complete enough to support product generation, archive, and traceability. If a format is missing required fields, is not from an approved source, or doesn’t pass basic structural checks, it should be rejected or held for review rather than accepted as good input.

Routine support should handle straightforward issues like locating an order, explaining a product, or resolving a single-user delivery problem. Anything that changes access, interprets policy, involves restricted data, or suggests a security problem should be escalated to the appropriate operations or security contact. If the issue could indicate a broader integrity problem, such as repeated bad deliveries or suspicious access patterns, it should go straight to escalation rather than being worked as a normal help ticket.

If an input is only missing minor metadata or has a recoverable structural issue, it should be corrected and resubmitted after the problem is fixed. If the question is whether the data itself is scientifically valid, or whether it came from the right source and time window, that should go to manual review and approval by the operations or science authority. Anything that is corrupted beyond recovery, from an unauthorized source, or impossible to reconcile with traceability requirements should be permanently discarded and logged so we can explain why it was rejected.

The system should provide a clear catalog of the standard NPOESS-derived products that are intended for broad operational use, plus the NOAA-specific products needed for NOAA missions. I’d expect the catalog to be organized by product family, sensor or observation type, and use case so users can tell quickly what’s available and whether it is current, archived, or restricted. I don’t have the exact list of products, but the catalog should be complete enough that users can search, request, and understand what each product is for without having to call support every time.

A product should be considered timely and reliable enough for immediate use when it is delivered within the required latency window, passes the defined quality checks, and the source data and processing status are both complete. If the product arrives late, is based on partial input, or has known anomalies that don’t invalidate it completely, it should be marked provisional or withheld from operational decision-making until reviewed. Anything that fails critical validation, has unresolved calibration or integrity issues, or cannot be trusted for an operational call should be routed for later use, correction, or manual review instead of being presented as ready.

The decision should come down to how much the product would affect an operational user if it were slightly imperfect versus how harmful a delay would be. If the data are basically complete and the issue is minor, release it immediately with a clear provisional or degraded-quality flag. If a short delay is likely to fix a known error without missing the decision window, then hold it briefly; if the correction would miss the usefulness window or the product has an unresolved critical defect, it should be held back until the next cycle.

Delivered products and order responses should include enough integrity information for the user to confirm they got the right content, such as a checksum, delivery identifier, or other verification token tied to the order. The system should run its own checks before release and again during distribution so we can catch corruption or mismatches early. If verification fails, the system should not treat the item as successfully delivered; it should retry if that looks like a transport issue, otherwise flag the order for support and preserve the audit trail. If the check cannot be completed, the response should be marked indeterminate and the user should be told not to rely on it until it is verified.

If the product is incomplete but still usable for some purposes, it should be labeled clearly as partial or provisional, with a note describing exactly what is missing and what limitations that creates. If the missing pieces affect only narrow use cases, it can still be distributed with a cautionary status and an explicit warning that it is not for full operational use. If the missing data undermines the product’s validity or could mislead users, it should be held back until the gaps are filled and the product can be reissued in a complete form.

If the failure looks like a transient delivery problem, the system should retry automatically a limited number of times. If the same failure repeats or the check suggests corruption, mismatch, or a bad package, it should escalate to support and keep the order flagged as unresolved. If we can’t confirm delivery at all, the order should stay in a non-delivered state until someone verifies it or the customer receives a corrected replacement.

The packaging should say plainly that the item is partial or incomplete, and it should identify the missing component, time segment, or processing step in simple terms. It should also state the limitation right in the delivery note, such as “restricted use only,” “not for full operational decision-making,” or “provisional pending completion,” depending on the impact. If it is safe for limited use, that needs to be explicit too, so users know what they can and cannot rely on without having to interpret the status themselves.

It should include whatever verification details we do have, like the order ID, delivery timestamp, package version, and any checksum or receipt reference that was already generated before the failure. If only part of the verification succeeded, the notice should say that clearly, for example “partially confirmed,” and specify which piece is still pending. If none of it can be checked, the response should be marked unverified and the user should be told to treat it as not authoritative until recovery and confirmation are complete.

Records should be eligible for archive transfer once they have been fully processed, verified, and released as the final accepted version, unless there’s an operational hold or a customer support issue tied to them. I don’t know that we’ve fixed a single universal retention period yet; that would need to be set by NOAA policy and any legal or scientific retention requirements. In practice, I’d expect the system to keep them locally until that retention window expires and the archive transfer has been confirmed successful.

An operational hold should go on the record if there’s an unresolved integrity problem, a disputed order, an incomplete product issue, or any failed delivery that still needs correction. We’d also hold it if the record is tied to a support case, a reprocessing request, or a known upstream data issue that could affect the final archive copy. In short, if there’s any doubt that it’s the final authoritative version, it should stay on hold.

The formal confirmation should be a positive acknowledgement from the archive destination that the record was received and validated, not just that it was sent. That confirmation needs to be stored in the system against the record, and any downstream order or support workflow tied to it should be updated so staff can see the transfer is complete. If the destination can’t provide that acknowledgement, we shouldn’t treat the transfer as closed.

I don’t know the exact retention rules yet, because those need to come from NOAA records management, legal, and the science program owners. In general, I’d expect the default to be whatever the formal records schedule says, and then extend it if there’s litigation hold, an audit, a quality investigation, or a reprocessing event tied to the record. I wouldn’t shorten it ad hoc in the system; if anything changes, it should come from an approved policy decision.

Yes, there could be an exception process, but it should be very tightly controlled. My expectation is that only an authorized records or program manager, with legal or compliance input when needed, could approve releasing a held record for archive transfer, and that approval should be logged. If the hold is due to integrity or legal issues, I’d be very cautious about allowing any override at all.

A manager should only release it if the hold is not about an unresolved legal matter or a known integrity defect, and the business owner agrees the record is ready to be archived despite the hold. If legal, compliance, or records management reviewed it, their approval or objection should be captured too, along with the release reason, date and time, approver identity, the specific hold being lifted, and any conditions attached to the release. That way we can show who made the decision and why if it is reviewed later.

If a release is approved, any conditions should be explicit and narrow, like “archive now but retain a copy in source until the audit completes” or “transfer only this product version, not later revisions.” Yes, the system should record separate concurrence or objection from legal, compliance, or records management whenever they reviewed it, because their position matters even if the final decision is made by the manager. If they did not review it, that should be recorded too so it is clear they were not part of the approval.

The system should handle the basic help directly, like product descriptions, metadata, usage notes, status, and order history, so users can answer routine questions without waiting on a person. If the issue is more specialized, like interpreting a scientific product, resolving a failed order, or explaining an anomaly, it should route to a support team with the right expertise. Yes, some catalog entries should be restricted by role or mission, especially sensitive or pre-release products, and those access rules should be enforced by the system rather than left to the user.

Beyond sensitive or pre-release items, I’d expect restrictions for products tied to specific missions or customer agreements, anything under legal hold, and anything with export or security limitations. If a user tries to access one of those entries, the system should deny the request cleanly, show that the item is restricted, and give only the appropriate next step, like contacting the support or authorization group. It should not reveal the protected content or more detail than necessary.

If a user keeps requesting the same restricted item, challenges the restriction, or indicates an operational need that might qualify for an exception, the system should escalate it to the support or authorization team rather than just stopping at a denial. I’d also want escalation if the request comes from an account that looks like it may have the wrong role assignment or if there’s a time-sensitive mission impact. The system should still block access until someone with authority reviews it, but it should preserve the context so the reviewer can decide quickly.

Yes, we’d expect some customer-group rules in addition to the general restriction types, especially where access depends on contract terms, a named customer account, partner status, or geographic limits. The system should allow access only when the user’s account matches the authorized group and the request is within the contract or mission scope; if it does not match, it should deny by default or route it for authorization review if there’s a plausible business case. Anything involving region, partner role, or account mismatches should be checked against the entitlement rules before any product details are exposed.

If the mismatch is clear and there’s no existing entitlement or approved exception on record, the system should stop with a denial. If the user can point to an active contract, mission exception, or a pending approval that might cover it, then it should send the request for authorization review instead of ending it outright. I’d also route it for review when the rule is ambiguous or the account data looks incomplete, because those are situations where a human needs to confirm the entitlement.

In most cases it should block access immediately and only show a generic restriction notice with the appropriate contact or next step. I wouldn’t want it to reveal partial product content for restricted categories unless there’s a very specific business rule saying a safe subset can be shown, and I’m not aware of one yet. So the default should be no partial disclosure, just enough information to guide the user without exposing the restricted item.
